meta.description: Not a Plato quote in his own words. The line is an 1857 gloss by philosopher William Fleming characterizing Plato’s Laws, Book X.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Atheism is a disease of the soul, before it becomes an error of the understanding'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Plato’s wording. It is an 1857 paraphrase by William Fleming summarizing Plato’s Laws Book X, which does call atheism a “disease.”

answer.label: Not a Plato quote — a Victorian paraphrase
answer.authorDates: Plato c. 428–348 BC · wording from William Fleming, 1791–1866
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Platonic — in Laws, Book X Plato calls atheism a “disease” and blames it on incontinence of pleasures before intellect. But this exact sentence is not a translation of Plato: it is Scottish philosopher William Fleming’s own gloss, printed as “a fine observation of Plato in his Laws” in his Vocabulary of Philosophy (1857), p. 52.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Vocabulary of Philosophy, Mental, Moral, and Metaphysical
Plato, Laws, Book X (4th c. BC)
Plato quoted via Jowett; the sentence itself is Fleming’s English

source.excerpt: It is a fine observation of Plato in his Laws — that atheism is a disease of the soul before it becomes an error of the understanding.
trail: The exact line first appears in William Fleming’s Vocabulary of Philosophy (1857), p. 52, where he calls it “a fine observation of Plato in his Laws” — his paraphrase, not a translation.
Secularist George Holyoake repeated it in The Limits of Atheism (1874), p. 13, again crediting Plato’s Laws.
Plato’s Laws, Book X (Jowett) does call atheism a “disease” and blames incontinence of pleasures — the source of the idea Fleming compressed.
Fleming’s line was carried into S. Austin Allibone’s Prose Quotations from Socrates to Macaulay (1880) and from there into the modern quote sites that now label it a bare “Plato” quote.
source.excerptNote: As written by William Fleming, Vocabulary of Philosophy (1857), p. 52 — his summary of Plato, presented as an “observation,” not a quotation.
source.rightsNote: Both layers are long out of copyright: Plato’s Laws is ancient, and the specific English wording comes from William Fleming’s Vocabulary of Philosophy (1857) — first published well before 1931, and Fleming died in 1866. Public domain in the United States.

author.heading: About Plato
author.metaLine: c. 428–348 BC · Athenian philosopher, founder of the Academy
author.bio: Plato was an Athenian philosopher and student of Socrates whose dialogues shaped Western thought. His last and longest work, the Laws, includes in Book X a sustained argument against atheism, treating disbelief in the gods as a moral and spiritual disorder — a “disease” rooted in unrestrained appetite — rather than a purely intellectual mistake. That argument is the seed a 19th-century editor later compressed into the popular one-liner.

copyAttribution: "Atheism is a disease of the soul, before it becomes an error of the understanding." — wording by William Fleming, Vocabulary of Philosophy (1857), glossing Plato's Laws, Book X. Not a direct quotation of Plato.

misattribution.heading: How it became a “Plato quote”
misattribution.intro: The line is real, but it was written in Victorian Scotland, not ancient Athens. Fleming offered it as his summary of Plato; quote sites dropped him and kept Plato.

items.why: No translation of Plato’s Laws produces this sentence. It originates as William Fleming’s “fine observation of Plato” in his Vocabulary of Philosophy (1857).
Plato’s Laws, Book X does call atheism a “disease” and traces it to incontinence of pleasures before intellectual error — so the thought is fairly credited to him even though the phrasing is not.

misattribution.truthLine: A faithful Victorian paraphrase, not a quotation: the sentence is William Fleming’s (1857), distilling an argument Plato really makes in the Laws.

context.heading: Why the distinction matters
lead: Plato’s Laws Book X argues that unbelief is not first a failure of reasoning but a corruption of character: people are dragged into denying the gods by unrestrained pleasures, and only afterward build arguments to justify it. Fleming’s epigram captures that order — soul first, understanding second — more crisply than Plato ever put it.

That crispness is exactly why it circulates as a “Plato quote.” It reads like an aphorism, so the intermediary who actually composed it disappears, and a 19th-century philosopher’s summary gets promoted to an ancient primary source.
context.pull: Soul first, understanding second — Plato’s argument, Fleming’s sentence.
